clue.text: Yens or pounds on what may be followed by gangs with goolies?

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for pounds sterling (from Latin libra)

parts.words: what may be followed by gangs with goolies
parts.note: the scout campfire song goes 'Ging gang goolie goolie...', so a ging is followed by a gang and then goolies; plural here

explanation.surface: A cheeky question about whether yen or pounds are what come before rude gangs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yens' looks like the Japanese currency beside 'pounds', but it is the plural of yen, a craving. 'Ging Gang Goolie' is a nonsense song sung round the campfire by Scouts, much loved in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A yen is a yearning or strong desire, so yens are cravings, a plural noun matching the plural answer.

clue.text: See 5
Hit from Simon the reason for deferring to Charles in diary?

definitions.meaning: a hit single by Carly Simon, the Bond theme from The Spy Who Loved Me

definitions.text: the reason for deferring to Charles in diary?
definitions.meaning: Charles Pooter is the hero of the Grossmiths' comic novel The Diary of a ...; read whimsically, the reason to defer to him is that he, the '...', performs best

explanation.surface: A music quiz question linked oddly to some diarist called Charles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charles in diary' tempts towards Pepys and Charles II; the diary is The Diary of a Nobody, whose narrator is Charles Pooter, so the song title can be read as praise of Pooter.
explanation.definitionFit: Carly Simon's 1977 hit single carries exactly this title, so the song name is a direct identification.

clue.text: See 24
Live genera winding round poles

indicators.note: round means the scrambled letters go around the word for live
winding means the letters of genera are twisted into a new order

parts.note: to live is to be, so live gives BE
N and S are the north and south poles

explanation.surface: Living plant species twining their way up garden canes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'winding' scrambles the plant word and 'round' wraps it about the verb for live, with the two poles after. The whole clue also pictures climbing beans growing up canes.
explanation.definitionFit: Climbing varieties of this vegetable are living plants that twine around canes or poles, so the whole clue paints them.

clue.text: Some cook reported truck loading up 'reproductive material' for show

indicators.note: loading means the next piece is placed first, loaded on before the truck

parts.note: some means a little, a small amount of something
to fry is to cook in hot fat

indicators.note: up here means the word for the genetic stuff is turned backwards

parts.note: DNA is the genetic material passed on in reproduction

indicators.note: reported means the word for truck is said aloud and spelt as the name it sounds like

parts.note: a lorry is the British word for a truck

explanation.surface: Seems to describe a cook hearing about a lorry hauling genetic samples to an exhibition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns DNA into AND, and 'loading' puts it before the truck; 'reported' changes LORRY (British for truck) into the surname it sounds like.
explanation.definitionFit: This was a BBC sketch comedy series starring Stephen Fry and Hugh Laurie, so it is an example of a television show.

clue.text: Summers' limits may/may not be important to these

definitions.text: Summers' limits may/may not be important to these

indicators.note: read as 'imported to', the letters are brought inside the word for these flowers

parts.note: in the surface, these are flowers, so blooms

indicators.note: limits means only the outer letters of the word Summers are taken

explanation.surface: Muses whether the edges of summer matter to some flowers or not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'important to' is read as 'imported into': S and S, the limits of 'Summers', go into BLOOMS. 'may/may not' plays on may, the hawthorn's flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: Flowers on trees and shrubs, such as hawthorn's may, are called by this name, and their season is bounded by summer.

clue.text: Weaving threads, set up prosecution

indicators.note: up in a down entry means the word for set is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a hen sets or sits on eggs, so set gives SIT
suing is taking legal action, a prosecution

explanation.surface: A weaver at work while a lawsuit is being prepared.
explanation.definitionFit: To tissue is an old verb for weaving fine fabric, especially with threads of gold or silver, so it means weaving threads.

clue.text: Only thirds needed, awful exams botched on the spin: call Mensa? No!

indicators.note: only the third letter of each of the next three words is wanted

parts.note: heads is a call made when a coin is spun

explanation.surface: A student who botched exams laments scraping thirds and rules out joining Mensa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thirds' looks like a degree class, but it takes the third letters F, A, T.
explanation.definitionFit: Mensa is the club for people of high IQ; the dimwits who would never be invited are idiots.

clue.text: Like the Invincibles, 12 19 22?

definitions.meaning: Arsenal's 2003-04 Invincibles went the whole league season without losing a game
the linked phrase says eggs stay as eggs, i.e. not whisked or broken

explanation.surface: Compares a famous undefeated football team with a proverbial saying.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading uses 'beaten' in the kitchen sense: eggs that remain plain eggs have not been whisked.
explanation.definitionFit: An undefeated team never lost, and eggs left as they are have not been whisked: both senses of never beaten.

clue.text: See 2
Treatment of indigos, perhaps, with I

definitions.text: Treatment of indigos, perhaps, with I

parts.note: I is the chemical symbol for iodine

indicators.note: treatment means the letters are worked on and rearranged

explanation.surface: Describes dyeing or treating blue indigos chemically with iodine.
explanation.definitionFit: To iodise is to treat something, such as salt, with iodine, whose symbol is I, so the whole clue describes the process.

clue.text: Militant aggresses with gas? I guess it's inevitable

indicators.note: militant means combative, so the following letters fight their way into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone resigned to the idea that a violent aggressor will resort to gas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Militant' looks like a noun, the aggressor, but is the anagram signal for AGGRESSES, GAS, I and GUESS together.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying expresses certainty, that something is bound to happen, so it matches an inevitable outcome.

clue.text: Missile launcher? Sound alarm when leading in lord

indicators.note: in means the run of letters goes inside the word for a lord

parts.note: a peer is a member of the nobility, a lord

indicators.note: leading means the word for when comes in front of the alarm sound

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as he left'
to hoot is to sound a horn as a warning

explanation.surface: Sounds like a warning given as a missile system is brought into a nobleman's house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Missile launcher' suggests military hardware; it is a child's toy tube for blowing dried peas.
explanation.definitionFit: A child's tube that fires dried peas launches small missiles, a playful description signalled by the question mark.

clue.text: Firm put off, with hidden dangers in store

parts.note: to deter is to put off or discourage
ground that is mined has explosives hidden in it, dangers waiting

explanation.surface: A business discouraged by risks lurking ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like a company; it is the adjective meaning resolute.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm resolve is a resolute, unwavering one, so firm here means resolute.

clue.text: Badly miscue, potting one ball at either end in sports venue

indicators.note: potting means taking in, so the jumbled word holds the next letters
badly means the letters of miscue are jumbled
only the first and last letters of the phrase one ball are taken

explanation.surface: A snooker player miscues and pots a ball at each end of the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'potting' puts O and L, the ends of 'one ball', inside the scrambled MISCUE.
explanation.definitionFit: A coliseum is a large stadium or arena, after the Roman amphitheatre where games were held.

clue.text: Having no time for empty-palmed occupants of singles bar?

definitions.meaning: without a date, a point in time, written on it
a date palm bearing no fruit is without its dates
people in a singles bar have no romantic partner for the evening

explanation.surface: Singles at a bar with no time and nothing in their hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'empty-palmed' suggests empty hands; it is a date palm without fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Undated, lacking fruit from the palm, and lacking a romantic partner are all senses of being without dates.

clue.text: A squalid place to have suspended herb for Spooner

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner's habit of swapping first sounds means the starts of the two words change places

parts.note: hung means suspended
dill is a feathery herb

explanation.surface: Hanging herbs to dry in a grubby corner.
explanation.definitionFit: A heap of manure is filthy, and figuratively the word means a degraded, sordid place.

clue.text: Dark film cast left in a screw steamer

indicators.note: in means the trimmed coating goes inside the word for a

parts.note: a means one

indicators.note: cast means thrown off, so the letter for left is shed

parts.note: plaque is a thin film, as on teeth
SS is the abbreviation for screw steamer, a ship driven by propellers

explanation.surface: A gloomy film being shot aboard a steamship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dark film' looks like one phrase; 'Dark' alone is the definition, as a noun, and 'film' is a coating such as dental plaque. 'cast' sheds the L for left.
explanation.definitionFit: The dark, as a noun, is absence of light; something light cannot pass through has that quality.

clue.text: Despite my opinion seeming big-headed, slimy and offensive, it's easy to misconstrue

indicators.note: to misconstrue is to read wrongly, so the letters are taken in the wrong order

explanation.surface: Someone admits their slimy, offensive view could easily be misread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and', 'it's' and 'to' only link; the fodder is SLIMY, OFFENSIVE and EASY.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a speaker's apology for boasting, used while praising one's own work despite sounding conceited.

clue.text: Gnats troubling soldier still

indicators.note: troubling means stirring up, so the insects' letters are disturbed

parts.note: a soldier ant is a worker caste of ant

explanation.surface: Insects bother a serviceman who keeps perfectly motionless.
explanation.definitionFit: Water that does not flow is motionless, so this adjective means not moving.

clue.text: See 24
Opponent of Saracens unusually scared about their game

indicators.note: about means the jumbled letters go round the game
unusually means the letters of scared are set out in an unusual order

parts.note: Saracens is an English rugby union club, and RU is rugby union

explanation.surface: Saracens rugby club's opponents are oddly afraid of how they play.
explanation.walkthrough: Saracens looks like the rugby club; the definition takes the word in its medieval sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Christian knights of the medieval Holy Land wars fought against Muslim Saracen armies.
